Field names and structure match the real artifact; every value here is

it carries filesystem paths, hardware identifiers, and footage metadata.
See docs/validation-method.md for what each group claims — and what it

source.redacted: race clip metadata removed — duration/resolution/fps are the only public facts

funnel._comment: person_detections, not detections: no bib detector exists in this pipeline (docs/decisions.md D2). 205 is how many runners were found; each one becomes an ROI attempt whose crop is computed from keypoints.

performance.frame_of_reference: offline pass; ~3x the clip length, not 3x realtime

_comment: Two counters per track, kept apart for the reason reference/frame_voting.py
prints them apart: a runner is visible in more frames than the runner is
readable in. `visible_frames` is the tracker's count. `read_frames` is the
voting count, and it is null here because per-track read counts are not
republished - the clip total (98) is in `funnel`. Collapsing the two into
one number is how a track gets credited with reads it never made.

tracks._comment: 17.5 s at 0.1 s sampling = 176 samples in the window; 141 of them show this runner. Not 141 reads: the whole clip produced 98.

Two reads is below the voting threshold in isolation (min_evidence=5 in reference/frame_voting.py defaults), and it is published anyway - because the candidate set is constrained before the crop is read, not after. The event's timing system says which bib numbers were on course in that second; a read that agrees with one of them is not a guess with weak support, it is a confirmation. This is the difference between a raw vote and a vote against a bounded candidate set, and it is why an unattended pipeline can publish a track a human would have thrown away.

failure_categories.action: archive; contested vote routes to arbitration

per_frame_log._comment: the real artifact holds one entry per sampled frame; two synthetic rows show the shape
